text: Zofia Emilia Kielan-Jaworowska (25 April 1925 – 13 March 2015) was a Polish paleobiologist born in Sokołów Podlaski, Poland. In 1928, her family moved to Warsaw when her father, Franciszek Kielan, was offered a job with the Association of Agriculture and Trade Cooperatives, a stay lasting five years; they returned to Warsaw in 1934 and lived in Żoliborz. After the war, when Warsaw was destroyed by the Nazis, the Department of Geology was among the ruins, and she attended lectures by Polish paleontologist Roman Kozłowski in his home, sparking her passion for paleontology. She earned a master's degree in zoology and a doctorate in paleontology from Warsaw University, later becoming a professor there. In 1948, she began working as an assistant in the University of Warsaw's Department of Paleontology, teaching paleontology to students in biology and geology, and completed her master's research on trilobites in the Świętokrzyskie Mountains, collecting over one hundred specimens over several summers. She received her master's degree in 1949 and worked at the university until 1952. From 1963 to 1971, she led Polish-Mongolian paleontological expeditions to the Gobi Desert, returning seven times, and unearthed numerous dinosaurs and mammals from the Cretaceous and early Tertiary periods. In 1965, her team shipped over 20 tons of fossils back to Poland; one notable find in 1971 was a Protoceratops and a young Velociraptor tangled in a struggle, with the fossilization process of their position still debated. Her research shifted from Paleozoic invertebrates, especially trilobites (studied from 1949 to 1963), to Mesozoic mammals in 1963. She authored the book *Hunting for Dinosaurs* (written in Polish and translated to English, published in 1969), which details her work in the Gobi Desert, her interactions with Mongolian people, and the hardships she faced, and co-authored *Mammals from the Age of Dinosaurs*, which won the Prize of the Foundation for Polish Science in 2005 for a creative synthesis of Mesozoic mammalian evolution. Her work was widely published in peer-reviewed journals, books, and monographs. She served as director of the Institute of Paleobiology from 1960 to 1982, then held a visiting professorship at the Musée national d’Histoire naturelle in Paris (1982–1984), followed by a professorship at the University of Oslo (1986–1995), becoming Professor Emerita in 1995. She was awarded the Walter Granger Memorial Award in 1988, the Romer-Simpson Medal in 1996 (the 8th recipient), the Commander's Cross with Star of the Order of Polonia Restituta in 2002, and the Righteous Among the Nations Medal in 1999. She was a member of the Polish Geological Society, Academia Europaea, Palaeontological Association, Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters, Norwegian Paleontological Society, Polish Academy of Sciences, and an honorary member of the Linnean Society of London, Polish Copernicus Society of Naturalists, and the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology. She also worked at Harvard University (1973–1974), Paris Diderot University (1982–1984), and the Polish Academy of Sciences. Several extinct animals were named in her honor, including Deinocheirus, Gallimimus, Kielanodon, Zofiabaatar, Kielantherium, Zofiagale, and Indobaatar zofiae. She married Zbigniew Jaworowski, a professor of radiobiology, in 1958. She was the first woman to serve on the executive committee of the International Union of Geological Sciences. In her obituary in *Nature*, Richard L. Cifelli noted that "Much of what we know about the origin and early evolution of mammals stems, directly or indirectly, from [her work]". Her co-author, Zhe-Xi Lou, stated that her contributions to paleontology are unmatched by any living expert and that only George Gaylord Simpson would be her equal in the field of Mesozoic mammalian studies over the past century, describing her as a rare leader and charismatic figure who improved both the science and the community of paleontology. During World War II, she helped hide two Jewish women with her family.
